attacks.claim: The announcement promises SMS for every cardholder, but the artifact says juvenile cards never see the option. The public statement is inaccurate and could mislead patrons about who receives texts.
attacks.evidence: Announcement text says exactly: "Text alerts for holds, for every cardholder." vs. "juvenile cards do not show it, and guardians can opt in with their own number"

attacks.claim: Consent records are deleted within 30 days if SMS is withdrawn. Consent records are the main evidence of TCPA-style consent for a 10DLC SMS program, and deleting them removes that defense. No retention period for consent records is defined.
attacks.evidence: "If SMS is withdrawn permanently, numbers and consent records are deleted within 30 days and patrons are emailed."

attacks.claim: The $900 cap covers only SMS. When it is hit, every opted-in patron falls back to automated phone calls, which are not capped or budgeted. A large opt-in base could create uncapped voice spend, and the budget memo does not cover it.
attacks.evidence: "On cap, texts stop and every opted-in patron falls back to their previous notice method (email or automated phone call...)" with budget "~$460/month... (approved, budget memo BM-26-14)"

attacks.claim: Hold activity is exposed to third parties and linked to identities. The provider keeps message logs for 30 days, and those logs include the body (branch, hold count, and the locker code). The internal log ties patron id to branch and delivery status. This sits uneasily with the stated no-borrowing-history policy, and the artifact does not address it.
attacks.evidence: "it retains message logs 30 days" and "Oak St locker. Code 482913, pick up by Sat Nov 14"; log stores "patron id, branch, channel, and delivery status"

attacks.claim: Locker accessibility features (high-contrast mode, audio guidance, adjustable text) are claimed but not tested. Screen-reader testing covers only the opt-in web form, and locker acceptance testing is not described as covering accessibility.
attacks.evidence: "audio guidance through a headphone jack, and adjustable text size" vs. QA "Opt-in form with NVDA + Firefox, VoiceOver iOS; 320/768/1280 px layouts" (no locker row)

attacks.claim: Key rollout claims rest on unprototyped conditions. The pilot covered 64 staff cards only, with no live teen, guardian, or Spanish traffic. The spend-cap fallback was tested at a $5 cap, not at forecast or real volume. The 38,000 texts/month forecast has no opt-in uptake basis.
attacks.evidence: "Staff pilot week (64 staff cards, real holds)" and "Spend cap reached (test cap $5)" and "Forecast 38,000 texts/month"

attacks.claim: The locker pickup code is delivered over SMS, so anyone with access to the phone or lock-screen previews can obtain it. The card-based path is only partly protective, and the artifact does not discuss this exposure.
attacks.evidence: "Code 482913, pick up by Sat Nov 14" with "enters the code" as the second factor

attacks.claim: The rollback remap was tested on 1,200 rows, but production locker volume is not stated. Already-sent codes become invalid on remap, and the notice to patrons is described only as a location change.
attacks.evidence: "tested in staging on 1,200 rows" and "patrons are notified of the new location"

attacks.claim: Queued texts are released at 08:00 across 14 branches, which creates a burst. The artifact gives no provider throughput or queue drain limit for this.

The template hardcodes the pickup date and assumes one locker location per batched message. A batched message combining holds at different locations or deadlines would be wrong, and the artifact does not specify how this is handled.
attacks.evidence: "2 holds ready at Oak St locker... pick up by Sat Nov 14" and "extra holds are batched into one message"
